prohibited_recommendations: Do not continue to treat the shoulder as isolated adhesive capsulitis (further glenohumeral corticosteroid injections or capsular procedures) once parkinsonism is identified

Do not prescribe centrally acting anticholinergics (trihexyphenidyl, benztropine) in a patient over 70 or with cognitive impairment
required_recommendations: Diagnose clinically probable PD (MDS 2015): left-predominant bradykinesia with decrement, cogwheel rigidity and a left-hand rest tremor, no absolute exclusion, no red flag; rest tremor is the one supportive criterion (the smell loss is self-reported, not tested), and the response to levodopa may add a supportive criterion [Postuma_2015]

Explain to the patient and family that the refractory left 'frozen shoulder', the lost arm swing, the micrographia and the slowness are parkinsonian rigidity and bradykinesia rather than primary adhesive capsulitis or cervical spondylosis, and stop further shoulder corticosteroid injections

Start carbidopa-levodopa 25/100 mg, half a tablet three times daily with food, increasing over 2 to 4 weeks to one tablet three times daily (300 mg/day levodopa), and review the response after 2 to 3 months [NICE_NG71]; at 73 with a MoCA of 24/30 prefer levodopa to a dopamine agonist
Measure lying and standing blood pressure before and during levodopa titration and review whether tamsulosin and amlodipine are both needed, since both add to orthostatic falls

Advise bedroom safety for the dream enactment (protect his wife, pad the bedside, remove sharp objects); if treatment is needed prefer melatonin, since clonazepam adds sedation, confusion and fall risk at his age

differential.key_features: Shoulder stiffness refractory to two injections and 12 weeks of physiotherapy, preceded by loss of arm swing, with ipsilateral rest tremor, decrement, cogwheel rigidity and micrographia: a primary shoulder disorder does not explain the syndrome

C5-C6 spondylosis on a prior spine MRI, but strength 5/5, no dermatomal sensory loss, normal upper-limb reflexes, no Hoffmann sign or clonus; spondylosis does not cause rest tremor, bradykinesia or micrographia
His tremor is a 4-5 Hz rest tremor that re-emerges after movement, with bradykinesia and rigidity; the mother's undiagnosed late-life 'shaking hands' does not make ET the cause
Dream enactment and parkinsonism with MoCA 24/30, but no fluctuations or visual hallucinations and no cognitive loss of daily function: no dementia
Only minimal small-vessel change (Fazekas 1) without basal ganglia infarct; asymmetric upper-limb onset with rest tremor, not a lower-body predominant stepwise syndrome

Light-headedness on standing on tamsulosin and amlodipine, but no orthostatic hypotension on measurement, no urinary incontinence, no cerebellar signs, rest tremor present, and normal putamina, pons and middle cerebellar peduncles on MRI
Full vertical eye movements, no falls, limb-predominant asymmetric signs and a normal midbrain on MRI

key_clinical_evidence: Left-predominant bradykinesia with decrement, cogwheel rigidity and a 4-5 Hz left-hand rest tremor that re-emerges after movement, with hypomimia, hypophonia and micrographia: parkinsonism by the MDS entry criterion [Postuma_2015]
Loss of left arm swing two years ago, then left shoulder stiffness refractory to injections and physiotherapy: an early parkinsonian presentation misread as adhesive capsulitis

No absolute exclusion and no red flag (no cerebellar sign, full vertical gaze, no falls, no dopamine-blocker exposure); rest tremor is the one supportive criterion, so the diagnosis is clinically probable PD until the levodopa response is known [Postuma_2015]
MRI without vascular, hydrocephalic or atypical-parkinsonism features; the bilateral nigrosome-1 loss on SWI is consistent with nigral degeneration [Schwarz_2014]
Self-reported smell loss, constipation and wife-reported dream enactment are prodromal non-motor features; the smell loss is not a supportive criterion until tested with a validated test [Berg_2015]
C5-C6 spondylosis with mild foraminal narrowing and a normal neurological examination of the arm for root or cord signs: an incidental structural anchor

patient.history_present_illness:
Mr. Kim is a 73-year-old right-handed Korean-American retired accountant who is referred to neurology by his orthopedic surgeon for persistent left shoulder stiffness and left arm movement difficulty that has not responded adequately to treatment for adhesive capsulitis over the past 18 months. He is accompanied by his adult son, who provides additional history.

Approximately two years ago, the patient and his family noticed that he no longer swung his left arm when walking. He and his wife attributed this initially to getting older. About 18 months ago he began experiencing left shoulder aching and stiffness with restricted range of motion. He was evaluated by orthopedic surgery, who diagnosed left-shoulder adhesive capsulitis based on restricted passive and active range of motion. Plain films showed no fracture; ultrasound showed no rotator cuff tear. He received two corticosteroid injections into the left glenohumeral joint and completed 12 weeks of physical therapy. His shoulder range of motion improved only marginally. A cervical spine MRI ordered at that time demonstrated C5-C6 spondylosis with mild foraminal narrowing, which the spine team considered unlikely to account for the shoulder-predominant picture. The orthopedic surgeon noted on his most recent visit that the shoulder stiffness had a different quality than typical frozen shoulder — the arm just did not move naturally — and has now referred him to neurology.

On direct neurological questioning today, the patient and his son report that over the past 12 to 15 months the patient's left hand has developed an intermittent trembling at rest, which stops when he reaches for something and returns when his hand is in his lap. He has noticed increasing difficulty with fine motor tasks on the left: buttoning shirts is labored, and his handwriting has become smaller. His son notes that his father appears to move more slowly in general, takes longer to rise from chairs, and shuffles more than before. The patient reports diminished sense of smell over the past two years, which he had not previously mentioned to any physician. He also reports worsening constipation and occasional lightheadedness when standing quickly. His wife has told him that he sometimes acts out his dreams at night — she has been kicked twice. He denies hallucinations, significant cognitive decline beyond mild word-finding difficulty, and denies any falls to date.

He takes no medications known to cause parkinsonism. He has never taken antipsychotics, metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, or promethazine.

neurological_exam.additional: Glabellar reflex positive (Myerson sign, fails to habituate). Handwriting sample shows micrographia with progressive diminution of letter size. Seborrheic dermatitis on forehead and nasolabial folds. Orthopedic range-of-motion documentation (brought by patient) notes left shoulder 'frozen' with 90-degree abduction limit; two prior corticosteroid injections with partial short-term benefit only.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose testing intact bilaterally without dysmetria; movements mildly slow on the left. Heel-to-shin testing intact. No cerebellar ataxia.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal, round, and reactive to light, 3 mm bilaterally. Visual fields full to confrontation. Extraocular movements intact; blink frequency reduced. Mild hypomimia with masked facies. Facial sensation intact bilaterally. Hearing grossly intact. Palate elevates symmetrically. Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius strength 5/5 bilaterally. Tongue midline without atrophy or fasciculations.
neurological_exam.gait: Gait notable for absent left arm swing (right arm swing reduced but present), mildly shortened stride length with left predominance, slight forward-flexed trunk posture. Initiation of gait mildly hesitant. No frank festination. Pull test: two steps backward with unaided recovery. Turns require 4-5 steps.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented to person, place, time, and situation. Speech mildly hypophonic with slightly reduced volume. Language fluent in English and Korean; mild word-finding pauses. Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) 24/30, losing points on attention/concentration (1), sentence repetition (1), verbal fluency (1), delayed recall (1), and abstraction (2). No aphasia, neglect, or apraxia.
neurological_exam.motor: Bulk normal throughout. Cogwheel rigidity at the left wrist and left elbow, more pronounced than the right; mild rigidity at the right wrist. Bradykinesia prominent in the left upper extremity — reduced amplitude and speed of finger tapping, hand opening/closing, and pronation-supination on the left, with mild involvement on the right. Left hand rest tremor at 4-5 Hz, pill-rolling in character, re-emerges at rest after deliberate movement. No rest tremor observed on the right. Strength 5/5 throughout all extremities. Active left shoulder range of motion reduced to approximately 90 degrees of abduction (patient and orthopedics attribute this to adhesive capsulitis).
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 2+ bilaterally, triceps 2+ bilaterally, brachioradialis 2+ bilaterally, patellar 2+ bilaterally, Achilles 1+ bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally. No Hoffmann sign. No clonus.
neurological_exam.sensory: Light touch, pinprick, and proprioception intact in all four extremities. Vibration slightly reduced at bilateral great toes, consistent with age-related peripheral change. Romberg test negative.
